newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Zaire rebels won't negotiate with new PM.
newsitem.headline: Zaire rebels won't negotiate with new PM.

text.p: Zaire rebels on Tuesday said they would not negotiate with newly nominated prime minister Etienne Tshisekedi and would only deal directly with President Mobutu Sese Seko.
The opposition in parliament nominated Tshisekedi, Mobutu's arch-foe, on Tuesday as the new prime minister to steer Zaire through negotiations with the rebels, who hold a quarter of the country.

"We want to discuss with the person who has power, which is Mobutu and not with Tshisekedi. We want Mobutu to give up power," Raphael Ghenda, information commissioner in the rebel alliance, told reporters.
"Mobutu's prime minister has no power, Mobutu has the final say. For six years Tshisekedi has been running after Mobutu in order to be made prime minister."
Many Zairean politicians said they expected ailing Mobutu to move quickly to sign Tshisekedi's appointment into law to succeed prime minister Kengo wa Dondo, who resigned a week ago.

Presidential Movement leader Idambituo Bakata indicated on Tuesday that Mobutu would endorse the appointment of the man he sacked as prime minister in 1992. A sovereign conference reappointed Tshisekedi but Mobutu again dismissed him in 1993.

The rebel Alliance of Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Congo-Zaire warned Tshisekedi against taking the job, arguing that anyone under Mobutu can play no part in a rebel-led transitional government.

Ghenda said by accepting the post of prime minister Tshisekedi became an enemy of the rebellion but said he could not be ruled out of a post-war political settlement and would be allowed to stand for election.

"If the Alliance puts in place its democratic structures then political actors can have another chance," said Ghenda. "Tshisekedi or Kabila or whoever else must present themselves before the suffrage of the people."
Tshisekedi, 64, has popular support in Zaire but support for rebel leader Laurent Kabila has also grown in the face of rebel advances since October against the Zairean army.
Boosted by territorial gains the rebels are in a strong position as they head into talks with government delegates, scheduled for South Africa this week.
Kabila has repeatedly argued that non-violent opposition, espoused by Tshisekedi, has failed to unseat Mobutu as the ultimate authority in the sprawling state at the heart of Africa.
Rebel fighters say they are moving steadily deeper into Tshisekedi's central Kasai homeland and towards the diamond-mining regional capital Mbuji Mayi.

Kasai has for years been a centre of opposition and uses different money from the rest of the country since Tshisekedi called on his followers to boycott new banknotes issued under Mobutu's instructions in 1993.
Mobutu has ruled Zaire since a military coup in 1965 but is now ailing with cancer.
